commentary.seminaVerbi:
Saul’s collapse under light reads like the psyche’s forced reversal: the aggressor meets the wounded Other and discovers the “enemy” lives inside his own moral body. That voice—addressing him by name, identifying with his victims—resembles the Bhagavad Gita’s moment when Arjuna’s violence is arrested by a revelation that turns duty into surrender, and it echoes Sufi accounts of qabd and bast, contraction then expansion, where certainty breaks the self so a larger allegiance can form. Speculation: the three-day blindness has the shape of an initiatory limen found in shamanic illness and in Tibetan “bardo” imagery, not as doctrine but as a psychological grammar for dying to an old identity.

The bread-and-flesh insistence presses past metaphor into a demand for incorporation: life is not admired, it is eaten. That is close to the Vedic soma and the Dionysian sparagmos in Greek mystery religion, where a god is taken into the body so the body learns the god’s pulse; it also parallels the Jewish idea of internalizing Torah—Ezekiel’s scroll, later rabbinic language of words as food—except here the nourishment is not text but person. Speculation: Zen’s “eat when hungry” cuts the opposite way—no sacrament, only immediacy—yet it shares the same claim that reality must be taken in, not merely contemplated.

Ananias calling him “brother” looks like restorative justice before it is a program: the community risks touch, and touch rehumanizes. That resembles the African ethic of ubuntu and the Buddhist practice of metta toward an enemy, not as sentiment but as a reweaving of the social self. The “scales” falling suggests the Gnostic motif of ignorance as a film over the eye, but here the cure is communal mediation, not secret knowledge.
commentary.excursus:
Saul isn’t converted; he’s captured. The light is an ambush that strips him of the one thing his violence depended on: the clean distance between “me” and “them.” “Why persecutest thou me?” is a psychological trap, forcing the persecutor to feel his target as his own body. His blindness is not punishment but the first honest state he’s had: the collapse of certainty into bare need. Three days without food reads like withdrawal, the body resetting after an addiction to righteousness.

Ananias is the real moral center, because he feels the dread that the story wants to hurry past. He knows reputations, dossiers, the way men like Saul don’t change; he resists not out of stubbornness but out of self-preservation. Calling him “Brother” is not sweetness; it’s a high-risk act of imagination, the kind that can get you killed. The “vessel of election” line lands like cold bureaucracy: this instrument will be used, and the price is suffering. Saul is not spared; he’s repurposed.

John’s bread speech is the same coercion in another register. It’s not a gentle invitation to believe; it’s a demand to ingest what horrifies you. Eat flesh, drink blood, or you have no life. The crowd’s disgust is the honest response to intimacy pushed past comfort into taboo. Eternal life is promised through an act that feels like violence turned inward: you don’t admire the sacred from a safe pew, you swallow it, let it enter the gut, let it undo your boundaries. The dread is the point. Desire is trained by being made to cross a line you can’t uncross.

Taken together, the texts say: the divine doesn’t persuade, it invades. It takes the persecutor’s eyes, then feeds him a body. It creates disciples by dismantling autonomy and replacing it with a dependence so total it feels like possession. The miracle is not that Saul starts preaching; the miracle is that anyone, like Ananias, still dares to touch the man who once came to bind them.
commentary.synthesis: Christ identifies himself with his persecuted and converts by incorporation: into his Body through the Church and into his life through his flesh and blood. Election is ordered to mission and sealed by suffering, sustained by a real communion that grants resurrection.

gospel.text: The discourse binds eternity to a specific mode of participation: life is not merely promised, it is ingested. The argument escalates from gift (flesh) to effect (resurrection) to union (abiding), then seals itself by contrasting manna’s mortality with a food that carries the living source.

Objection targets plausibility; Christ answers with insistence on realism (‘indeed’) rather than explanation. The text prefers offense to dilution, making the hearer choose between literal scandal and literal dependence.

reading.text: The narrative moves from authorized coercion to commanded obedience. Saul’s initiative collapses into reception: he is halted, interrogated, then redirected into a mediated instruction—God chooses to convert the violent through a voice and to restore him through the Church.

Ananias supplies the communal obstacle: memory, reputation, institutional warrants. The resolution is not reassurance but commission; the community’s fear is overridden by a divine claim on the offender, forcing ecclesial incorporation to run ahead of moral comfort.
The endpoint is public speech in the very venues sought for arrests. The persecutor’s social capital is inverted into witness; the same synagogue network becomes the first stage of proclamation.

marginalia.text: Breath as weapon: zeal ventilated into policy; paperwork for violence.
The persecuted speaks as the Persecuted One: identity relocated into the Body.
Eyes opened to darkness; three-day fast: a forced liturgy of unmaking.
Election named as instrumentality; vocation calibrated in suffering, not privilege.
‘Brother’ precedes proof; touch breaks the spell; scales fall like verdicts.
Gift defined as flesh; scandal is not disbelief but mechanics: ‘How can…?’
Double amen turns metaphor into condition: life is gated by eating and drinking.
Mutual indwelling made alimentary; the Son’s dependence becomes the eater’s.
Manna as dead-end typology; heaven-bread that does not expire.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: We ask you, Lord, that since you have given us the grace to know the resurrection of your Son, you may also grant that the Holy Spirit, by his love, may raise us to new life. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, and is God for ever and ever.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer:
Let us pray:
Lord, almighty God: since by our rest we are going to imitate your Son who rested in the tomb, we ask you that, when we rise tomorrow, we may also imitate him by rising to a new life. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.

lines: And Saul, as yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest
And asked of him letters to Damascus, to the synagogues: that if he found any men and women of this way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
And as he went on his journey, it came to pass that he drew nigh to Damascus. And suddenly a light from heaven shined round about him.
And falling on the ground, he heard a voice saying to him: Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?
Who said: Who art thou, Lord? And he: I am Jesus whom thou persecutest. It is hard for thee to kick against the goad.
And he, trembling and astonished, said: Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?

And the Lord said to him: Arise and go into the city; and there it shall be told thee what thou must do. Now the men who went in company with him stood amazed, hearing indeed a voice but seeing no man.
And Saul arose from the ground: and when his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. But they, leading him by the hands, brought him to Damascus.
And he was there three days without sight: and he did neither eat nor drink.
Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus, named Ananias. And the Lord said to him in a vision: Ananias, And he said: Behold I am here, Lord.
And the Lord said to him: Arise and go into the street that is called Strait and seek in the house of Judas, one named Saul of Tarsus. For behold he prayeth.
(And he saw a man named Ananias coming in and putting his hands upon him, that he might receive his sight.)
But Ananias answered: Lord, I have heard by many of this man, how much evil he hath done to thy saints in Jerusalem.
And here he hath authority from the chief priests to bind all that invoke thy name.
And the Lord said to him: Go thy way: for this man is to me a vessel of election, to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel.
For I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake.

And Ananias went his way and entered into the house. And laying his hands upon him, he said: Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus hath sent me, he that appeared to thee in the way as thou camest, that thou mayest receive thy sight and be filled with the Holy Ghost.
And immediately there fell from his eyes as it were scales: and he received his sight. And rising up, he was baptized.
And when he had taken meat, he was strengthened. And he was with the disciples that were at Damascus, for some days.
And immediately he preached Jesus in the synagogues, that he is the son of God.

lines: If any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world.
The Jews therefore strove among themselves, saying: How can this man give us his flesh to eat?

Then Jesus said to them: Amen, amen, I say unto you: except you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. Except you eat and drink, etc... To receive the body and blood of Christ, is a divine precept, insinuated in this text; which the faithful fulfil, though they receive but in one kind; because in one kind they receive both body and blood, which cannot be separated from each other. Hence, life eternal is here promised to the worthy receiving, though but in one kind. Ver. 52. If any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever; and the bread that I will give, is my flesh for the life of the world. Ver. 58. He that eateth me, the same also shall live by me. Ver. 59. He that eateth this bread, shall liver for ever.
He that eateth my flesh and drinketh my blood hath everlasting life: and I will raise him up in the last day.
For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed.
He that eateth my flesh and drinketh my blood abideth in me: and I in him.
As the living Father hath sent me and I live by the Father: so he that eateth me, the same also shall live by me.
This is the bread that came down from heaven. Not as your fathers did eat manna and are dead. He that eateth this bread shall live for ever.
